parts: Lesson 5: Company Form of Business Organisation — Summary

A joint stock company (company) is a voluntary association of persons with a large and fluctuating membership, with a distinct legal personality; it is formed by registration under the Companies Act 2013. Prof. L.H. Haney: 'an artificial person created by law, having separate entity, with a perpetual succession and common seal'. It mobilises small savings (a share of face value Rs 10 lets a small saver become an owner).

Features: incorporated association (minimum seven members for a public company, two for a private company; Section 3 allows a One Person Company); legal entity distinct from its members; artificial person (acts through directors and officers); perpetual succession (members may come and go but the company continues); common seal (official signature; agreements executed on behalf of the company bear the seal); limited liability (liability of members limited to the unpaid amount on shares or the guarantee); transferability of shares (free in a public company, restricted in a private company); distinct pattern of management (elected representatives called directors, the Board of Directors).

Private company (Section 2(68)): restricts transfer of shares, limits the number of members to 200 (excluding employees), prohibits invitation to the public to subscribe to its securities; minimum two members; 'Private Limited' at the end of its name; exempt from many regulations. Types: One Person Company (OPC; Section 3(1)(c): only one member, adult natural person, Indian citizen and resident; relaxations: no cash flow statement, no AGM, only one board meeting in each half year with a gap of at least 90 days) and Small Company (Section 2(85): other than a public company, paid-up capital not exceeding Rs 50 lakh and turnover not exceeding Rs 2 crore). Public company (Section 2(71)): not a private company; can invite the public to subscribe to shares and debentures; minimum seven members, no maximum; free transfer of shares; 'Limited' at the end of the name; e.g. Reliance Industries, Bajaj Auto, SAIL. Under the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015 the minimum paid-up capital requirement was removed and all companies can commence business immediately on receiving the certificate of incorporation (Section 11 omitted).

Merits: large resources, limited liability, continuity of existence, benefits of large-scale operation, liquidity (shares traded on NSE and BSE, DMAT account), professional management, research and development, tax benefits. Limitations: difficult to form, control by a group, excessive government control, delay in decision making, lack of secrecy, social abuses (monopoly, influencing politicians, exploiting workers and consumers). A company is suitable where the volume of business is large, area of operation widespread, risk high, huge finance and professional management needed (banking, insurance).
Choosing the right form of business

Factors: ease of formation (sole proprietorship easiest, company needs many formalities); availability of large resources (company); liability or risk (unlimited in sole proprietorship and partnership, limited in company and co-operative); stability (company continues irrespective of death or insolvency); flexibility (maximum in sole proprietorship); secrecy (maximum in sole proprietorship, least in company); extent of state control (least in sole proprietorship and partnership, most in company).

Four stages: promotion, registration (incorporation), capital subscription and commencement of business. Promotion: discovery of an idea and taking action; a promoter conceives the idea and takes all measures to bring the enterprise into existence (Dhirubhai Ambani promoted Reliance); the promoter stands in a fiduciary position. Registration with the Registrar of Companies: Memorandum of Association (signed by at least 7 persons for a public company, 2 for a private company), Articles of Association (internal management rules), list of directors, written consent of directors, notice of registered office address (within 30 days) and statutory declaration. The Registrar issues the Certificate of Incorporation, the company's birth certificate, with the name, date and signature and seal of the Registrar, and allots a Corporate Identity Number (CIN).
Multinational company, joint venture and PPP

A multinational corporation is registered in one country but does business in several others through factories, branches or subsidiaries; features: centralised management, worldwide spread, better quality products, large size, access to the international market and special attention to advertisement (Hyundai, Coca-Cola, Sony). Advantages to host countries: foreign capital, employment, advanced technology, growth of ancillary units, increased exports and healthy competition; limitations: least concern for the host country's priorities, adverse effect on domestic enterprises, change in culture. Joint venture: two or more independent firms contribute capital and participate in operations for a specified purpose (Maruti Suzuki); features include access to advanced technology, optimum use of capital, pooling of resources and expertise, innovation and sharing of risk and reward. Public Private Partnership (PPP): partnership between the public and private sectors in financing, designing and developing infrastructure (power, transport, education, healthcare); features: for public benefit, government actively involved, higher priority projects, combined funds and expertise, shared risk; merits: faster implementation, higher quality, reduced costs, shared risk, funds from both; demerits: profit motive of private sector, leakage of secrets, delays due to conflicts.

Private sector enterprises are owned by individuals or groups and aim at profit maximisation; the Companies Act requires them to spend at least 2 per cent of average profit of the last three years on CSR. Public enterprises (PSUs) have 51 per cent or more shares held by the Central or State government; only three sectors are reserved for the government (railway, atomic energy, explosive material). Characteristics: state ownership and control, state financing, socio-economic objectives, public accountability (to Parliament; CAG reports), excessive formalities and autonomy or semi-autonomy. Objectives: rapid economic development through infrastructure, generating financial resources, redistribution of income and wealth, employment, balanced regional growth, development of small-scale and ancillary industries and export promotion and import substitution. Differences: private – objective profit, owned by individuals, managed by owners and professionals, capital from owners and public issues, operates in all areas with adequate return; public – objective social welfare and balanced development, owned and managed by government, capital from government funds, operates in basic and public utility sectors.

Forms of public enterprises: Departmental undertaking (run as a department of the government headed by a minister; railways, post and telegraph, broadcasting, munition factories; financed from the budget; subject to budgetary accounting and audit; merits: social objectives, responsible to legislature, control over economic activities, revenue to government, little scope for misuse of funds; limitations: bureaucracy, excessive parliamentary control, lack of professional expertise, lack of flexibility, inefficiency). Statutory (public) corporation: incorporated under a special Act of Parliament or State Legislature (SBI, LIC, IFCI, State Electricity Boards); autonomous, separate legal existence, capital provided by government, managed by a Board of Directors nominated by government, self-sufficient in finance; merits: professional management, internal autonomy, responsible to Parliament, flexibility, promotion of national interests, easy to raise capital; limitations: government interference, rigidity, ignoring the commercial approach. Government company (Section 2(45)): a company in which not less than 51 per cent of the paid-up share capital is held by the central or state government or both; registered under the Companies Act.
